approachQuestion.prompt: Encode a nested integer value as an exact string: integers use canonical decimal notation, and a list is [ followed by its child encodings separated by commas followed by ]. There are no spaces or trailing commas. Examples: [3,[],[-2,0]] encodes as "[3,[],[-2,0]]"; [] encodes as "[]"; -7 encodes as "-7".
constraints: A value is either a signed 32-bit integer or an ordered list of values; lists may be empty.
The input is finite, acyclic, and has no shared subobjects. There are n total integer and list objects, including the root, with 1 ≤ n ≤ 100000; maximum nesting depth is h ≤ 1000.
Do not modify the input. Indexing a list, reading a tag, and integer comparisons take constant time.
Canonical decimals use no plus signs or leading zeros, except zero itself is 0. Integer conversion has constant bounded cost for the fixed 32-bit domain.
Return a fresh character buffer. Appending one character costs amortized constant time.

options.text: Write only integer leaves and commas, omitting all list delimiters.
options.feedback: [[]] and [] must remain distinguishable even though both contain no integer leaves.

options.text: Use one shared output buffer. Write an integer directly; for a list write [, then each child in order with a comma before every child except the first, then write ].
options.feedback: Entry and exit delimiters surround exactly one list, and separators appear only between existing children.

options.text: Recursively build a separate immutable string for every child, repeatedly concatenate the growing prefix with each child and its delimiter, and return the complete root string.
options.feedback: This yields the exact format but copies growing prefixes and completed child strings unnecessarily.

options.text: Write a comma after every child, including the last child of each nonempty list.

feedback.reason: Emit delimiters and commas at their structural boundaries into one shared returned buffer.
details: Allocate one growable character buffer. At an integer append its canonical decimal digits. At a list append the opening bracket, recursively emit each child with a comma before all but the first, then append the closing bracket. Return that same output buffer, without converting or copying it into another representation.

Emit delimiters and commas at their structural boundaries into one shared returned buffer. Empty lists still require brackets. Repeatedly concatenating child strings would introduce copying absent from this fixed method.
“Write only integer leaves and commas, omitting all list delimiters.”: [[]] and [] must remain distinguishable even though both contain no integer leaves.

“Use one shared output buffer. Write an integer directly; for a list write [, then each child in order with a comma before every child except the first, then write ].”: Entry and exit delimiters surround exactly one list, and separators appear only between existing children.

“Recursively build a separate immutable string for every child, repeatedly concatenate the growing prefix with each child and its delimiter, and return the complete root string.”: This yields the exact format but copies growing prefixes and completed child strings unnecessarily.
“Write a comma after every child, including the last child of each nonempty list.”: [3] must encode as "[3]", not "[3,]".

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze method-1 as described in the revealed method. Let n and h have the meanings in Q1. Use child indices and references without copying lists. Count active call frames; exclude input and returned output. There is no tail-call elimination. No hashing is used. The output buffer including capacity is excluded; append is amortized constant time, and each fixed-width integer emits at most 11 characters. Choose the tightest worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair among the options.

feedback.reason: Emit each bounded-domain encoding character once with depth-sized delimiter state.
details: The encoding has a number of characters proportional to n for the bounded integer domain. Each is emitted once, while pending calls store only cursors and delimiter state.
“O(n) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: Nested calls remain active along a path; their storage must be counted.
“O(n²) time, O(h + 1) auxiliary space”: Each object is processed once without rescanning or copying its descendants.
“O(h + 1) time, O(h + 1) auxiliary space”: A shallow but wide input can still require inspecting every object.
